newsitem.title: CANADA: Spring weather key to Red River flooding-Manitoba.
newsitem.headline: Spring weather key to Red River flooding-Manitoba.

text.p: Floodwater levels in the Red River valley were forecast to be one to 1-1/2 feet higher than last year's flood based on normal spring weather, Manitoba Natural Resources Minister Glen Cummings said Friday.

"Spring weather conditions will play a critical role in determining the extent and severity of flooding. Precipitation for the month of March has been below average in Manitoba. However, it has been above average in the U.S. portion of the Red River watershed," Cummings said in a statement.
A rapid melt or heavy spring rain could see levels three to five feet higher than 1996 between the U.S. and Winnipeg.
Last year's flood delayed spring of wheat, barley, canola, flax and corn by one month, compressing the frost-free crop growing window. Canadian grains need 100 days frost free.
The Red River Valley accounts for two percent of Prairie acreage but 3.5 percent of grain output, the Canadian Wheat Board has said. Canada is a major supplier to world markets.

The U.S. portion of the Red River watershed saw three times the average annual snow accumulation this winter while the Canadian side saw twice the average accumulation. There is a 10 percent chance this could be the worst flood of the century, MNR has said.
Dikes around Red River towns should withstand the flood even under an adverse weather scenario, Cummings said.
But the towns of St. Adolphe, St. Jean, Letellier and Emerson may need to raise their dikes another two feet.
"If the decision is to proceed, it's anticipated that the work on the dikes will take seven to 10 days," Cummings said.
Significant flooding is expected in southeast Manitoba on the Brokenhead River, Whitemouth River and Whiteshell River.
Assiniboine River flooding between St. Lazare and Brandon was forecast to be similar to last year, Cummings said.
Souris River flooding near the U.S. border was projected to be similar to last year.
